paragraphs.title: Opening the Debate and Examining Job’s Claims

easy.explanation: The chapter begins, “Furthermore Elihu answered and said.”
easy.q: Who begins speaking in this chapter?

answers: Wise men and those with knowledge
easy.explanation: Elihu says, “Hear my words, O ye wise men; and give ear unto me, ye that have knowledge.”
easy.q: Whom does Elihu ask to listen to his words?

easy.explanation: Job is quoted as saying, “I am righteous.”
easy.q: What did Job say about his own righteousness?

answers: Choose judgment and examine the matter together
Let Job choose his own reward
medium.explanation: He says, “Let us choose to us judgment: let us know among ourselves what is good.”
medium.q: What does Elihu suggest they do before deciding what is good?

answers: The ear tries words as the mouth tastes food
medium.explanation: He says, “For the ear trieth words, as the mouth tasteth meat.”
medium.q: What comparison does Elihu make between the ear and the mouth?

answers: That it profited a man nothing
That it made a man king
medium.explanation: Elihu quotes Job as saying, “It profiteth a man nothing that he should delight himself with God.”
medium.q: What did Job say about delighting himself with God?

answers: So the claims can be examined together
So they can give Job wealth
So they can replace God as judge
challenge.explanation: Elihu calls on wise and knowledgeable people to help examine what is right.
challenge.q: Why does Elihu invite wise men to participate in the discussion?

answers: That Job’s wound was without transgression
That Job listened to wise men
challenge.explanation: Job says, “My wound is incurable without transgression.”
challenge.q: Which claim of Job does Elihu present as especially troubling?

answers: Every statement should be accepted immediately
Words should be tested before a decision is made
challenge.explanation: The comparison emphasizes testing and discerning words before reaching a conclusion.
challenge.q: What does the comparison of the ear and mouth teach about judgment?

easy.explanation: Elihu says, “Far be it from God, that he should do wickedness.”
easy.q: What must not be attributed to God?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “For the work of a man shall he render unto him.”
easy.q: According to what does God repay a person?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “If he gather unto himself his spirit and his breath.”
easy.q: What can God gather unto Himself?

answers: God does not act wickedly or pervert judgment
People are not responsible for their actions
medium.explanation: Elihu declares that God will not do wickedly and will not pervert judgment.
medium.q: What conclusion does Elihu draw from God’s just dealings with people?

answers: Give him according to his deeds
medium.explanation: The phrase means that God repays a person according to his work and ways.
medium.q: What does “render unto him” mean in this context?

answers: God can gather a person’s spirit and breath
medium.explanation: If God gathers a person’s spirit and breath, human life depends entirely on Him.
medium.q: What relationship does Elihu show between God’s power and human life?

answers: It describes man returning to dust
It describes man ruling the world
challenge.explanation: The passage says, “All flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust.”
challenge.q: How does the statement that all flesh perishes reinforce human dependence on God?

answers: God does not see human deeds
God repays according to a person’s work and does not pervert judgment
challenge.explanation: Elihu joins God’s just repayment with His refusal to pervert judgment.
challenge.q: What is Elihu’s central argument against the claim that God is unjust?

answers: God has authority over the whole world
challenge.explanation: The question attributes the ordering and authority of the world to God.
challenge.q: What does “Who hath disposed the whole world?” imply about God?

paragraphs.title: God Shows No Partiality and Rules the Powerful

easy.explanation: Elihu asks whether the one who hates right should govern, emphasizing God’s opposition to injustice.
easy.q: What does God hate according to Elihu?

easy.explanation: God does not accept the persons of princes or regard the rich more than the poor.
easy.q: Between whom does God show no partiality?

answers: All the ways and goings of man
easy.explanation: The passage says, “His eyes are upon the ways of man, and he seeth all his goings.”

answers: Break them and set others in their place
medium.explanation: Elihu says God can break mighty men and set others in their stead.
medium.q: What can God do to mighty men?

answers: God does not favor princes because of their rank
medium.explanation: The expression means that God does not show partiality toward rulers.
medium.q: What does “accepteth not the persons of princes” mean?

answers: There is no darkness or shadow of death where they can hide
They are always in the city
They want everyone to see them
medium.explanation: The text says there is no darkness or shadow of death where they may hide themselves.
medium.q: Why can workers of iniquity not hide from God?

challenge.explanation: God regards neither the rich nor princes more than the poor.
challenge.q: What quality of God’s judgment is emphasized by comparing princes and the poor?

answers: It enables Him to know and judge human actions
It gives man control over God
challenge.explanation: Because God sees all human ways, He knows their works and can judge them rightly.
challenge.q: How does God’s seeing every human way support His rule?

answers: Even the powerful are subject to God
challenge.explanation: God can break mighty men and set others in their stead, so their authority is not ultimate.
challenge.q: What does God’s ability to remove mighty men and replace them show?

paragraphs.title: Punishment of the Wicked and Hearing the Poor

easy.explanation: The passage says, “He striketh them as wicked men in the open sight of others.”
easy.q: Whom does God strike in the sight of others?

answers: The cry of the poor and afflicted
easy.explanation: The text says, “He heareth the cry of the afflicted.”
Elihu says, “That the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared.”
easy.q: Whom does God prevent from reigning?

answers: They turned back from God and would not consider His ways
medium.explanation: The wicked are condemned because they turned back from God and would not consider His ways.
medium.q: Why are the wicked punished according to these verses?

answers: God withholds His visible favor or intervention
medium.explanation: The expression describes God concealing His face and withholding apparent intervention.
medium.q: What does “hideth his face” mean in this context?

answers: The wicked turn away, God strikes them, and He hears the poor
The poor rule, and then the wicked disappear
The wise choose a king, and God hides
medium.explanation: The passage connects the wicked turning from God, their punishment, and God hearing the afflicted.
medium.q: Which sequence best describes the passage?

answers: Both show God protecting people from oppression
Both describe the strength of the wicked
challenge.explanation: God hears the vulnerable and prevents a hypocrite from ensnaring the people.
challenge.q: What connection is made between hearing the poor and preventing a hypocrite from ruling?

answers: The punishment is public rather than hidden
The punishment occurs only in a dream
The wicked become able to see
challenge.explanation: The phrase highlights the public nature of God’s judgment.
challenge.q: What does “in the open sight of others” emphasize?

answers: A God who hears the afflicted and opposes oppression
A God dependent on human rulers
challenge.explanation: The passage portrays God as hearing the poor, judging the wicked, and restraining harmful rulers.
challenge.q: What picture of God emerges from this passage?

easy.explanation: The passage presents a direct confession and request addressed to God.
easy.q: To whom does the person address his words?

easy.explanation: He says, “That which I see not teach thou me.”
easy.q: What does the person ask God to teach him?

easy.explanation: He says, “If I have done iniquity, I will do no more.”
easy.q: What does the person promise if he has done iniquity?

answers: Acknowledge chastisement, seek instruction, and stop offending
Choose a reward without asking God
medium.explanation: The speaker acknowledges chastisement, asks to be taught, and promises not to offend again.
medium.q: What is the proper response to suffering in this passage?

answers: I will not continue doing wrong
medium.explanation: The phrase expresses a resolve to stop sinning or doing wrong.
medium.q: What does “I will not offend any more” mean?

answers: To recognize hidden wrongdoing and stop it
medium.explanation: The request shows a desire to learn about faults that are not yet recognized.
medium.q: Why ask God to teach what the person does not see?

answers: Man should not insist on deciding his own recompense
challenge.explanation: Elihu challenges the idea that a person should determine how God must repay him.
challenge.q: What criticism is implied by “Should it be according to thy mind?”

answers: Acknowledging chastisement, seeking instruction, and avoiding further sin
Blaming God, rebelling, and choosing a reward
challenge.explanation: The passage presents a practical response of humility, instruction, and repentance.
challenge.q: How do the main ideas of this passage fit together?

answers: He recognizes his need for divine instruction
challenge.explanation: The request shows humility and willingness to receive correction from God.
challenge.q: What does “That which I see not teach thou me” reveal about the person’s attitude?

answers: Men of understanding and a wise man
easy.explanation: Elihu says, “Let men of understanding tell me, and let a wise man hearken unto me.”
easy.q: Who is asked to give an opinion about Elihu’s words?

answers: As the speech of a prophet
easy.explanation: Elihu says, “Job hath spoken without knowledge.”
easy.q: How does Elihu describe Job’s speech?

easy.explanation: The final verse says, “For he addeth rebellion unto his sin.”
easy.q: What does Elihu accuse Job of adding to his sin?

answers: To be tried unto the end
medium.explanation: Elihu says, “My desire is that Job may be tried unto the end.”
medium.q: What does Elihu say Job desires?

answers: Job’s actions occur in the presence of the gathered speakers
Job is among wise men as their leader
medium.explanation: The phrase places Job’s alleged conduct in the setting of the assembled group.
medium.q: What does “among us” indicate in “he clappeth his hands among us”?

answers: He treats the many words as evidence of poor understanding
He says the two are unrelated
medium.explanation: Elihu combines the charge of speaking without knowledge with multiplying words against God.
medium.q: What connection does Elihu make between Job’s lack of knowledge and his many words?

answers: So his claim can also be examined by understanding people
So they can replace Job with a king
So the debate will end immediately
challenge.explanation: Elihu invites wise listeners to evaluate and respond to his argument.
challenge.q: Why does Elihu ask discerning men to hear him?

answers: Job speaks and argues without sufficient understanding
Job is too gentle in his request
Job speaks only about the poor
challenge.explanation: Elihu repeatedly presents Job’s words as lacking knowledge and wisdom.
challenge.q: What is Elihu’s chief criticism of Job’s desire to be tried?

answers: Job adds rebellion to sin and multiplies words against God
Job moves from wisdom to silence
Job moves from poverty to wealth
challenge.explanation: Elihu accuses Job of adding rebellion to sin and increasing his words against God.
challenge.q: What escalation is described in the final verse?
